newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich downplays reports of GOP complaints.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich downplays reports of GOP complaints.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich, flanked by his top deputies, said Wednesday he was still in charge and played down reports of internal Republican complaints about his leadership.
"I went into the conference as speaker...They called me Mr. Speaker as I came out," the Georgia Republican said after a 2-1/2 hour closed door meeting of House Republicans.

Gingrich, who is largely credited with engineering the Republican resurrection to control of the House in 1994, has had a rocky tenure and barely won re-election as speaker in January. He was reprimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations.

"Newt's fine," House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio, told reporters. Kasich, Majority Leader Dick Armey and House Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer stood with Gingrich at the news conference.

A group of conservative House Republicans met Tuesday night in Armey's office to discuss their concerns about the leadership's response to President Clinton's veto of a popular bill to provide government help for flood victims.

Republican aides said they had been dismayed that the leaders seemed to walk right into the public relations fiasco and were worried the same could happen on the coming tax cut bill, which they have called the party's 'crown jewel'.

Clinton had warned repeatedly he would veto the bill if it arrived with two provisions unrelated to flood aid. It was sent to him anyway, he vetoed it and Republicans took a public thrashing from Democrats for a week before disaster aid went to the White House cleared of objectionable provisions.

A spokesman for Representative Steve Largent of Oklahoma, a lawmaker who attended both meetings, said it was "an intrafamily discussion" which would continue, but declined to discuss details of the meetings.

Chief among Republican concerns is the coming fight with the president over the five-year, $85 billion tax bill. Conservatives said they were fearful of losing voter support if Clinton succeeded in painting their party as advocates of tax cuts for the rich.
The Clinton administration has argued that more of its benefits should go to lower income people, chiefly by allowing a $500 per child credit to include families who owe no tax.
"Are we going to let him play class warfare?" an aide said.
In response to party concerns, Gingrich said they intended to keep the message to voters simple: "We are going to keep talking about cutting taxes rather than increasing welfare."

The House next week will take its first vote on the tax bill, which Armey said would help the middle class. "Seventy-five percent of the benefits go to people earning under $75,000 a year," the Texas Republican said. "It is a tax cut for people who pay taxes. The president wants to transform it into an income transfer package," he added.

At the White House, spokesman Mike McCurry took the high road on the subject of the Republicans' squabbles. "We have a lot of business to do and a lot of fish to fry, and it doesn't serve anyone's purposes if there are a lot of internal disagreements in the majority party in Congress."

Armey, who Tuesday declined several opportunties to defend Gingrich, stood at his side Wednesday. Armey had also said Tuesday he was not bound by the details of the budget agreement with the White House, but a day later said there was no doubt the Republicans would comply fully.
Representative Peter King, a New York Republican who has criticised Gingrich in the past, said the speaker's declining popularity had put the balanced budget agreement in danger.
"There is no doubt we are in a weakened position," King told Fox Television's Fox on Politics programme.
"The president is holding more of the cards than we are because of the fact that his ratings are higher than Newt's and Newt is not a popular leader," King said.
